usage: What you file at a police station, station office, or on LOST112 when something goes missing.
Verb form (분실 + 하다); the written/official counterpart of spoken 잃어버리다.
物 'object', so 분실물 = the lost thing; 분실물 센터 / 보관소 = lost-and-found.
Noun-before-분실 pattern; you can swap in 지갑·여권·카드 분실 the same way.
examples: 가방을 분실했어요.
I lost my bag.
Simplest frame: object + 을/를 + 분실했어요, the formal 'I lost ~'.
지하철에서 지갑을 분실해서 신고하러 왔어요.
I lost my wallet on the subway, so I came to report it.
-아서 links the loss to the reason you're at the counter.
혹시 여기 분실물 보관소가 어디예요?
Excuse me, where is the lost-and-found here?
혹시 + the signage word 보관소 is exactly how you'd ask staff at a big station.
nuance: 분실 is the Sino-Korean noun (紛失, 'scatter-lose') that officialdom uses on forms, kiosks, and signs like 분실물 보관소; it frames the loss as YOUR own carelessness, not someone else's act. The sharp contrast to learn is 분실 vs 도난: 분실 = you misplaced it yourself (no suspect, police just log it), whereas 도난 = it was stolen (a crime, police investigate). In speech most people still say the warmer 잃어버렸어요; reserve 분실하다 for reporting, writing, or reading signage, where it sounds appropriately crisp and formal. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 분실 like a verb you can attach to a person — you cannot say 사람을 분실했어요 for 'I lost a person'; 분실 only takes inanimate items, and even then you must add 하다 (분실하다) rather than saying bare 분실해요.

mistakes: Don't confuse 분실 (you misplaced it) with 도난 (it was stolen) — police log a 분실 but open a criminal case for a 도난, so the wrong word sends your report down the wrong track.
분실 is a noun; to verb it you must add 하다 (지갑을 분실했어요), and never use it about a person — 친구를 분실했어요 is wrong; for missing people Koreans say 실종.
In everyday conversation jumping straight to 분실했어요 can sound stiff; with friends 잃어버렸어요 is far more natural, and 분실 is saved for the official channel.

usage: Filed when an item was taken by someone — the criminal counterpart of a 분실 신고.
당하다 ('to suffer/undergo') marks YOU as the victim of the theft, not the thief.
Often seen in apartment-complex notices warning residents to lock up.
防止 'block-stop'; printed on locks, tags, and security stickers.
examples: 자전거를 도난당했어요.
My bike got stolen.
Core frame: object + 을/를 + 도난당했어요, the victim-marking form.
택배가 도난당해서 경찰에 신고했어요.
My parcel was stolen, so I reported it to the police.
-아서 ties the theft to the action you took next.
요즘 이 동네에 택배 도난이 많대요.
They say there's a lot of parcel theft in this neighborhood lately.
-대요 reports hearsay; 도난 stands alone here as a plain noun (no 하다).
nuance: 도난 (盜難, 'theft-calamity') means someone deliberately took your property, so the police open a criminal case instead of merely logging a missing item — that legal weight is the whole reason it contrasts with 분실 (you simply misplaced it). The grammar trap that catches every English speaker is the verb: you must say 도난당하다, where 당하다 marks you as the one who SUFFERED the theft; plain 도난했어요 literally reads 'I committed the theft' and accidentally confesses to the crime. Register-wise 도난 is the formal, report-and-signage word; in casual storytelling Koreans say 누가 훔쳐 갔어요 ('someone stole it and left'). Habitual partners are 도난 신고, 도난 방지, and 도난당하다, and you'll meet the noun on building notices long before you ever need to file the report yourself.

mistakes: Never say 도난했어요 to mean 'I was robbed' — 하다 makes you the actor, so it reads 'I committed theft'; the victim form is 도난당했어요.
도난 (stolen by someone) is not 분실 (you misplaced it); choosing wrong decides whether police investigate a crime or just file a lost report.
Don't attach 도난 to a person as the stolen object — it applies to your belongings; for a kidnapped person the word is entirely different (납치).

usage: The single most common compound; written as one solid word, 交通事故.
나다 is the intransitive 'occur' — nobody is blamed, it just happened.
내다 (transitive 'bring about') marks the subject as the one at fault.
現場 'present-spot' = the exact place it happened; police seal it off.
examples: 앞에서 사고가 났어요.
There's an accident up ahead.
Bare frame: 사고가 나다, the neutral 'an accident occurred', nobody blamed yet.
제가 사고를 내서 보험사에 전화했어요.
I caused an accident, so I called the insurance company.
사고를 내다 openly admits fault; the 가/를 swap is the whole meaning.
사고가 나면 먼저 112에 신고하세요.
If there's an accident, report it to 112 first.
112 is the police line; 119 is fire/ambulance — memorize both.
nuance: 사고 (事故, 'matter-incident') covers any sudden harmful event — car crashes, workplace mishaps, falls — and is the umbrella word a 교통사고 or 산업재해 sits under. The make-or-break contrast is purely grammatical and Koreans listen for it: 사고가 나다 (with 가) means the accident merely HAPPENED, assigning no blame, while 사고를 내다 (with 를) means the subject CAUSED it and is therefore liable — get the particle wrong and you may accidentally confess fault at the scene. Compare also 사건, which is an 'incident/case' in the investigative or criminal sense (a 살인 사건 is a murder CASE), whereas 사고 leans toward unintended mishap. Natural partners are 교통사고, 사고가 나다/내다, 사고 현장, and the everyday 접촉사고 (a minor fender-bender).

mistakes: Don't mix up 사고가 났어요 (an accident happened) with 사고를 냈어요 (I caused one) — the 를 version admits liability and your insurer will treat it differently.
사고 is the EVENT, not the people; the injured person is a 피해자 and the at-fault driver a 가해자 — never call a person a 사고.
Don't reach for 사건 when you mean an everyday crash; 사건 implies a criminal/investigative 'case', while a road bump is a 사고 (or 접촉사고).

usage: Used for accidents, disputes, and out-of-court deals between two parties.
金 'money' — the sum paid to settle, especially after an accident or assault.
書 'written document' that both sides sign to make the deal binding.
보다 here means 'work out/settle' — the colloquial verb of choice.
examples: 상대방하고 합의를 봤어요.
I reached a settlement with the other party.
합의를 보다 is the everyday spoken phrasing; 상대방 = the other party.
합의금으로 백만 원을 받기로 했어요.
We agreed I'd receive one million won as a settlement.
-기로 하다 marks the agreed-upon terms; 합의금 is the payout.
경찰서에서 합의서를 작성하고 사건이 마무리됐어요.
We filled out the settlement agreement at the police station and the case wrapped up.
합의서 + 작성하다 is the set phrase; settling often closes a minor case.
nuance: 합의 (合意, 'unite-intention', literally 'minds joined') is enormous in Korean accident and minor-crime culture: reaching 합의 with the victim — usually with 합의금 changing hands and a signed 합의서 — frequently reduces a sentence or makes the prosecutor drop the case entirely. The boundary learners blur is 합의 vs 동의: 합의 is a two-way deal where both parties negotiate and CONCEDE to a middle ground (often money, often legal), whereas 동의 is one-sided AGREEMENT that you accept someone's opinion or request ('I agree, that's fine'). It also differs from 약속, an everyday promise about plans. Register is formal-to-neutral, at home in police stations, insurance calls, and contracts. The English-speaker pitfall is using 합의했어요 for casually agreeing on dinner plans — that needs 동의했어요 or 그러기로 했어요; 합의 implies a negotiated, often compensated settlement.

mistakes: 합의 (a negotiated, usually compensated settlement) is not 동의 (agreeing with an opinion) — 'I agree with you' is 동의해요, never 합의해요.
Saying 합의했어요 implies the deal is final and concluded; if you're still bargaining, say 합의 중이에요 (we're in the middle of settling).
Don't use 합의 for casual plan-making ('let's agree to meet at six') — that's 약속하다 or 그러기로 하다; 합의 carries legal/financial weight.

usage: 내다 is the verb for paying penalties and fees; never 주다.
刑 'sentence' — a 벌금형 is a criminal sentence served by paying money rather than jail.
State the amount right after 벌금, no particle needed.
告知書 'notification document' = the official payment slip mailed to you.
examples: 벌금을 냈어요.
I paid a fine.
Bare frame: 벌금을 내다; 내다 (not 주다) is the only natural verb for paying penalties.
음주운전으로 벌금이 많이 나왔어요.
I got a heavy fine for drunk driving.
-(으)로 gives the cause; 나오다 = (a charge) is issued/comes out.
벌금 고지서가 집으로 와서 깜짝 놀랐어요.
The fine notice came to my house and gave me a fright.
고지서 arrives by mail; -아서 links the surprise to receiving it.
nuance: 벌금 (罰金, 'punishment-money') is a criminal-court fine imposed after a court finds you committed an actual offense, so it rides a completely different legal track from 과태료, the administrative penalty for petty rule-breaking. Koreans draw this line sharply: a 벌금 leaves a record that you were criminally penalized (a 벌금형 is literally a criminal sentence), while a 과태료 — like an illegal-parking charge — carries no such stain. The fixed verb is 벌금을 내다 ('pay'); the English-speaker trap is 벌금을 주다, which uses 'give' and makes it sound like you're handing over money as a gift or donation. Note too that 벌금 is the specific monetary penalty, whereas 처벌 is the broader concept of punishment (jail, suspension, fine) that a 벌금 is just one instance of. You'll most often hear it paired with 내다, 나오다 (it 'came out' = was issued), and 고지서.

mistakes: Don't swap 벌금 (criminal court fine) with 과태료 (administrative penalty like illegal parking) — a 벌금 means a court found you guilty, so the wrong word overstates the offense.
Use 벌금을 내다, not 벌금을 주다; 주다 ('give') makes it sound like a voluntary gift rather than a penalty you owe.
벌금 (a specific money fine) is not 처벌 (punishment in general); a 벌금 is one TYPE of 처벌, so don't treat the two as interchangeable.

usage: Standard verb is 내다, the same as for any fee or penalty.
駐車 'parking'; the most common reason a city resident ever gets one.
賦課 'levy-charge' = the act of officially charging it to you.
The slip mailed to you stating the amount and deadline.
examples: 과태료가 나왔어요.
I got hit with a fine.
Simplest frame: 과태료가 나오다 = a fine is issued/comes out against you.
불법 주차로 과태료를 냈어요.
I paid a fine for illegal parking.
-(으)로 marks the cause; 과태료를 내다 is the set verb phrase.
기한 안에 내면 과태료가 좀 깎여요.
If you pay within the deadline, the fine gets reduced a bit.
Early payment usually earns a discount; 깎이다 = to be cut/reduced.
nuance: 과태료 (過怠料, 'excess-negligence-fee') is a LIGHT administrative penalty for breaking minor non-criminal rules — illegal parking, a late 전입신고, missed reporting deadlines — and crucially it does NOT make you a criminal or leave a criminal record. That is the entire dividing line versus 벌금: a 벌금 is a court fine for an actual offense, whereas a 과태료 is just an administrative charge an office levies on you. Residents bump into 과태료 most often through parking tickets and late move-in registration, and many can be paid online with an early-payment discount. The verb is 과태료를 내다 (or it 나오다, 'comes out'). Two pitfalls: English speakers over-dramatize it by translating it as 'fine' and equating it with 벌금, and the spelling trips people up — it is 과태료 with 태 in the middle, NOT 과대료; the syllable is 怠 'negligence', not 大 'big'.

It's 과태료, not 과대료 — the middle syllable is 태 (怠, negligence), and learners constantly misspell and mispronounce it as 대.
Don't say 과태료를 주다 ('give a fine'); like all penalties it takes 내다 (pay) or 나오다 (be issued).

english: civil complaint / public petition or request
usage: 넣다 'to put in' = to submit a 민원; also 민원을 제기하다 (more formal).
接受 'receive' = what the office does when it logs your 민원.
室 'room' = the desk/counter at a 구청 that handles public requests.
The online portal (it absorbed the old 민원24) where many 민원 are now filed.
examples: 주민센터에 민원을 넣었어요.
I filed a request at the community center.
민원을 넣다 is the everyday verb; 주민센터 is your local office.
층간소음 때문에 민원이 많이 들어와요.
Lots of complaints come in about noise between floors.
들어오다 = (complaints) come in; 때문에 gives the cause.
민원을 제기하려면 신분증이 필요합니다.
To lodge a civil complaint you need an ID.
민원을 제기하다 is the formal register; -(으)려면 = 'in order to'.
nuance: 민원 (民願, 'people-wish') is any official request OR complaint a citizen submits to a public office — issuing a document, reporting a pothole, asking the 구청 to act — and it is the formal channel through which ordinary Koreans interact with bureaucracy. The key thing English speakers miss is its breadth: it is NOT only a 'complaint'. Contrast it with 불만, which is mere personal dissatisfaction or grumbling with no formal status; a 민원 is the official, logged, trackable submission, so context (a request vs a grievance) decides the tone. It is a neutral, administrative word, common in 민원실, 민원 접수, 민원 처리. The pitfall is the verb: say 민원을 넣다 or the formal 민원을 제기하다, never bare 민원을 하다, which sounds unfinished — 민원 needs a 'submit/raise' verb, not the generic 하다.

Use 민원을 넣다 or 민원을 제기하다, not 민원을 하다, which sounds incomplete; 민원 pairs with submit/raise verbs.
Don't assume 민원 always means 'complaint' — it equally covers neutral requests like getting a certificate issued, so don't read hostility into it.

usage: 在職 'holding a post'; proves you work somewhere, needed for visas and loans.
떼다 literally 'detach/tear off' — the idiomatic verb for pulling an official copy.
發給 'issue-give' = official issuing; the word on kiosks and government sites.
所得 'income'; proof of earnings, often required for rent or a visa.
examples: 증명서를 한 통 떼야 해요.
I need to get one copy of a certificate.
통 is the counter for documents/letters; 떼다 = obtain a copy.
증명서는 무인 발급기에서 뽑을 수 있어요.
You can print certificates at the self-service kiosk.
무인 발급기 = unmanned issuing machine; 뽑다 = print/pull out.
은행에서 소득증명서를 요구해서 정부24에서 발급받았어요.
The bank asked for an income certificate, so I issued it on Gov24.
-아서 links cause and action; 발급받다 = receive an official issuance.
nuance: 증명서 (證明書, 'prove-clarify-document') is the catch-all suffix for official proof papers — 재직증명서, 소득증명서, 출입국사실증명서 — and the headword you attach a topic to. The detail that ambushes learners is the verb: Koreans say 증명서를 떼다, where 떼다 literally means 'to detach/tear off' (from the days of tearing a page off a register), so 'get a copy' is idiomatically 'detach a certificate'; the equally correct formal verb is 발급받다 ('receive an issuance'). Do NOT say 증명서를 만들다 ('make a certificate'), which implies you forged it yourself rather than having an authority issue it. Distinguish 증명서 from 신분증: a 증명서 PROVES a fact (your job, income), whereas a 신분증 is an ID CARD proving who you are — they are not interchangeable. Most 증명서 can now be pulled from a 무인 발급기 or 정부24 without queuing at a counter.

mistakes: 증명서 (a proof-of-fact document) is not 신분증 (an ID card) — don't use one when you mean the other; they serve different purposes.
Say 증명서를 떼다 or 발급받다, not 증명서를 만들다 — 만들다 ('make') implies you created/forged it yourself instead of an office issuing it.
Don't drop the topic prefix when a specific one is needed: a bank wants a 소득증명서 or 재직증명서, so bare 증명서 can be too vague at the counter.

usage: Seen on roadside posters: 목격자를 찾습니다 ('seeking witnesses').
陳述 'statement' = the account a witness gives to police.
Put the event before 목격자: 사고 목격자, 범행 목격자.
目擊 'eye-strike' = to see an event happen with your own eyes.
examples: 혹시 목격자세요?
Are you by any chance a witness?
혹시 softens a direct question to a stranger; -세요 is the polite 'are you ~?'
목격자가 있어서 처리가 빨랐어요.
There was a witness, so it was handled quickly.
-아서 links cause and result; witnesses speed up claims and reports.
제가 그 사고를 목격해서 진술하러 왔어요.
I witnessed that accident, so I came to give a statement.
목격하다 = to have seen it happen; pairs naturally with 진술하다.
nuance: 목격자 (目擊者, 'eye-strike-person', the one who 'struck it with their eyes') is the eyewitness who actually SAW an incident — a key word around 교통사고 and crime, and you'll spot 목격자를 찾습니다 posters near accident spots. The role contrast to nail is 목격자 vs 피해자 vs 가해자: a 목격자 merely observed and was not harmed, a 피해자 is the one who suffered, and a 가해자 caused it — confusing them scrambles who police talk to and why. Register-wise the verb 목격하다 is markedly more formal than plain 봤어요 and signals you witnessed something report-worthy. That is also the pitfall: don't use 목격하다 for casually 'seeing' a friend or a movie — that is just 보다 or 만나다; reserve 목격하다 for accidents, crimes, and incidents serious enough to testify about.

mistakes: 목격자 (eyewitness) is not 피해자 (victim) — a witness saw the event but wasn't harmed, so don't swap the two when explaining your role.
목격하다 is for incidents and events only; for casually seeing a friend say 봤어요/만났어요 — 친구를 목격했어요 sounds absurd, as if you spotted them at a crime scene.
Don't say 목격자를 봤어요 to mean 'I witnessed it' — YOU are the 목격자; the verb you want is 목격했어요.

usage: 被害者 'suffer-harm-person' = the harmed party in an accident or crime.
加害者 'add-harm-person' = the one who caused it; learn the pair together.
입다 'to wear/sustain' is the fixed verb; the root noun is 피해.
補償 'make-good' = righting the harm, usually with money.
examples: 저는 이 사고의 피해자예요.
I'm the victim of this accident.
Core frame: 저는 ~의 피해자예요, establishing your role when reporting.
가해자가 보험으로 처리해 준대요.
The at-fault party says they'll handle it through insurance.
Contrast 가해자 with 피해자; -(으)ㄴ대요 reports what they said.
피해를 입은 만큼 보상을 받을 수 있어요.
You can get compensation in proportion to the harm suffered.
-(으)ㄴ 만큼 = 'to the extent that'; pairs 피해 with 보상.
nuance: 피해자 (被害者, where 被 marks the PASSIVE 'one who is harmed') always pairs with its mirror 가해자 (加害者, 'one who adds harm'); the 被 vs 加 character literally encodes who receives versus who inflicts, and knowing which you are shapes liability, insurance, and who owes whom. The base noun 피해 means 'damage/harm' and combines widely — 피해를 입다, 피해 보상, 재산 피해 — so master the noun and the family follows. It is standard, neutral legal vocabulary, not a dramatic word like English 'victim' can feel; Koreans use it matter-of-factly in reports. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb for suffering damage: it is the fixed collocation 피해를 입다 (using 입다, the same verb as 'to wear', here 'to sustain'); 피해를 받다 with the generic 'receive' is much less natural in this set pairing and marks you as a learner.

Use 피해를 입다 for suffering damage; 피해를 받다 is unnatural in this fixed collocation, even though 받다 means 'receive'.
피해자 is neutral legal vocabulary — don't avoid it as too harsh; in a report calling yourself the 피해자 is simply stating your role, not melodrama.

usage: 陳述 'lay out-state' = to formally recount events to police or in court.
書 'document' = the paper that records your account, signed by you.
From the officer's side: the police 진술을 받다 from you.
A witness's formal account of what they saw.
examples: 사실대로 진술했어요.
I stated it truthfully.
사실대로 = 'as it really is'; the cleanest frame for 진술하다.
경찰서에서 진술서를 작성했어요.
I wrote out a statement at the police station.
진술서 + 작성하다 is the set phrase for putting it in writing.
통역사를 통해 진술하고 싶은데요.
I'd like to give my statement through an interpreter.
A right worth knowing as a foreigner; -(으)ㄴ데요 softly opens the request.
nuance: 진술 (陳述, 'lay-out and state') is your FORMAL account of what happened, given to police or written as a 진술서, and it carries far more weight than ordinary 말하다 because it can become evidence in a case. The contrast learners need is 진술 vs 설명: 설명 is a neutral 'explanation' you give anyone about anything, while 진술 is specifically a statement to authorities with legal consequences — use 진술 only in official contexts. As a foreign resident, remember you can request a 통역사 (interpreter) before you 진술하다; the police 진술을 받다 ('take' your statement) while you 진술하다 ('give' it). The nastiest pitfall is the near-homophone 진실 (眞實, 'truth'): 진술 (a statement, which may or may not be true) is NOT 진실 (the truth itself), and a 진술서 (statement document) is not a 진실서. One syllable, completely different word.

mistakes: 진술 (a formal statement to authorities) is heavier than 설명 (a casual explanation) — use 진술 only in police/legal contexts, not for explaining your weekend.
It's 진술, not 진실 (truth) — they sound nearly identical but a 진술 is your account (true or not), while 진실 is the actual truth; 진술서 ≠ 진실서.
Don't say 경찰이 진술했어요 when the police TOOK your statement — the officer 진술을 받다, the person being questioned 진술하다.

usage: 處罰 'handle-penalize'; subject is usually the law or authorities.
받다 marks YOU as the one penalized — the passive side.
水位 'water-level' used figuratively = the degree/level of the penalty.
刑事 'criminal' (as opposed to 민사, civil) punishment.
examples: 음주운전은 강하게 처벌받아요.
Drunk driving is punished severely.
처벌받다 from the offender's side; 강하게 = severely/harshly.
처벌을 원하지 않는다고 진술했어요.
I stated that I don't want them punished.
A real choice a victim can make to soften a minor case; -다고 reports your statement.
불법 주정차도 처벌 대상이에요.
Illegal parking is also subject to penalty.
처벌 대상이다 = 'to be a target/subject of punishment'.
nuance: 처벌 (處罰, 'handle-and-penalize') is the legal PUNISHMENT itself — the whole category of sanctions, from a fine to imprisonment — and pairs with crimes and serious violations. The boundary with 벌금 is the one to fix: 벌금 is one specific FORM of 처벌 (a monetary court fine), whereas 처벌 is the umbrella concept that also includes jail (징역) and suspension, so they are part-and-whole, not synonyms. A culturally crucial phrase is 처벌을 원하지 않는다 ('I do not wish them punished'), which a 피해자 can state to soften or drop a minor case — tightly linked to 합의. The active/passive split is the grammar pitfall: use 처벌받다 (with 받다) when YOU are the one penalized, and 처벌하다 when the authority is doing the punishing; saying 처벌했어요 about yourself wrongly casts you as the punisher, not the punished.

mistakes: Don't say 처벌했어요 about yourself when you mean you were punished — that makes you the one inflicting punishment; the correct form is 처벌받았어요.
처벌 (punishment in general) is not 벌금 (a specific fine) — a 벌금 is just one kind of 처벌, so don't use them as equals.
Don't confuse 형사 처벌 (criminal punishment) with 민사 (civil matters); 처벌 belongs to the criminal/penal side, while civil disputes seek compensation, not 처벌.
